    <t s="13">And he continues in the discourse,</t>
    <t s="14">that the beginning of the psalm is "L-rd, You have been a dwelling place for us, etc." and the end of the psalm6</t>
    <t s="15">is "And let the pleasantness of the L-rd our G-d be upon us, etc.",</t>
    <t s="16">"Maon" (dwelling place) and "Noam" (pleasantness) are the same letters.</t>
    <t s="17">And one must understand the connection of these three matters</t>
    <t s="18">(the relevance of the psalm to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev,</t>
    <t s="19">that this psalm was composed by Moshe, and the connection of "Maon" and "Noam").</t>
    <t s="20">Also, one must understand why he brings a proof from the Midrash that this psalm was composed by Moshe,</t>

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that Psalm 90, "A prayer of Moshe," is connected to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev, as the Alter Rebbe recited it on that day, and that Dovid received a tradition that Moshe composed it, raising questions about the connection between these themes.

translations.translation: "A prayer of Moshe, the man of G-d, etc."1,
And the Rebbe, my father-in-law, explains in his well-known discourse2
that this psalm relates to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev
[It is known that the Alter Rebbe would recite a daily portion of Tehillim according to the division for the days of the month3,
and since the psalm "A prayer of Moshe" is the beginning of the monthly Tehillim portion for the nineteenth day of the month,
he therefore recited this psalm on his day of redemption
(Yud-Tes Kislev)
And he continues in the discourse,
that Dovid, king of Israel, had a tradition4
that this psalm was composed by Moshe,
as it is brought in the Midrash5
that Moshe said eleven psalms corresponding to the eleven tribes.
And he continues in the discourse,
that the beginning of the psalm is "L-rd, You have been a dwelling place for us, etc." and the end of the psalm6
is "And let the pleasantness of the L-rd our G-d be upon us, etc.",
"Maon" (dwelling place) and "Noam" (pleasantness) are the same letters.
And one must understand the connection of these three matters
(the relevance of the psalm to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev,
that this psalm was composed by Moshe, and the connection of "Maon" and "Noam").
Also, one must understand why he brings a proof from the Midrash that this psalm was composed by Moshe,
when in the psalm itself it is stated that it is "a prayer of Moshe."

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev began the spreading of the wellsprings outward, connecting Moshe as the first and final redeemer, and that the eleven psalms correspond to the level of "One and not in number" drawn into the ten Sefiros, especially into Malchus, whose ultimate revelation will be in this physical world for the purpose of a dwelling place for the Awtsmoos.

translations.translation: B)
And it can be explained based on what is known7
that with the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev, the matter of "Your wellsprings shall spread forth outward" began,
which is the preparation and vessel for "the master has come, the King Moshiach"8.
Based on this,
the relevance of this psalm to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev indicates
(also)
its relevance to the future redemption.
And this is why, after stating in the discourse that this psalm relates to the redemption of Yud-Tes Kislev, he continues that this psalm was composed by Moshe,
for Moshe is the first redeemer and he is the final redeemer9.
[And he specifies that Dovid, king of Israel, had a tradition that this psalm was composed by Moshe,
for in this he hints
that the aspect of Moshe relevant here is that Moshe redeemed Israel from the Egyptian exile,
for the redemption from Egypt is a preparation for the future redemption10
through Dovid, the King Moshiach,
as it is written, "As in the days of your exodus from the land of Egypt, I will show him wonders"11].
And he brings the statement of the Midrash that Moshe said eleven psalms,
for in the number eleven there are two matters.
One, that before
(and above)
ten is the Ein Sof, which is above the ten Sefiros,
"You"12
are One and not in number13,
and eleven is the drawing down of the One
(the One and not in number)
into the ten,
into all ten Sefiros14
and even into the Sefirah of Malchus.
And on the contrary,
the primary drawing down of the aspect of "One and not in number" is into Malchus,
for the root of Malchus is in the innerness of Kesser.
For all the Sefiros have their root in the externality of Kesser, which is counted in the count of ten Sefiros15,
and the root of Malchus is in the innerness of Kesser, which is not counted in the count of the Sefiros15,
"One and not in number."
However, in revelation,
Malchus is lower than all the Sefiros,
to the extent that it descended to become the source for the existence of the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah16,
even down to this physical world.
And in the future to come, there will be a revelation of the root of Malchus
(the "One and not in number")
within Malchus
[and particularly as it descended into Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah16]
and through this—in the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, even in this physical world,
and on the contrary,
the primary revelation will be in this physical world,
and through this the intention of a dwelling place in the lower worlds17 will be completed,
that this lower world, below which there is no lower18,
will be a dwelling place for Him, blessed be He,
for Him, for His very Essence (Awtsmoos)19.
